Interesting: the Washington Post says that Jensen Huang's downfall was Marco Rubio's doing (https://t.co/4YahEGer9Q), and it looks like the "spy" framing was directly his and not the CIA's.

As they write, Rubio took a CIA report and rewrote it in a memo "in his own more assertive terms." 

Which fits neatly with CNN reporting that the CIA is "not yet convinced" that Alice Huang was a spy (https://t.co/Cd5PTbKqfG): if the CIA is not convinced, yet a memo rewritten from the CIA’s own report presented her as a spy, then there’s only one person who could have turned "not convinced" into "spy": the man who did the "more assertive" rewriting, aka Marco Rubio 🤷

The WaPo article also mentions the motive: China hawks like Rubio had spent years trying to "destroy the influence Jensen had over the president", and WaPo calls his ouster "a huge victory" for them as it allows them to "seize on the moment to redirect the national agenda toward tougher policies on China."

And, as a matter of fact, they’re already pushing three new chip-restriction bills into the defense bill now that Jensen is no longer around to lobby against them.

If true, it means the real "influence operation" targeting Jensen was run out of Washington, not Beijing 🤷

I think Musk gets something about Jensen that most ignore. The guy was practically running an industrial planning operation across half the AI supply chain. Convincing tiny suppliers to expand factories, reserve capacity, commit billions in capex and trust that $NVDA would be there to buy the output. 

Some of those relationships were apparently built on a handshake because his personal credibility was effectively being used as economic collateral.

Now imagine you're a substrate or advanced packaging supplier. Jensen convinced you to reserve most of your capacity for $NVDA, perhaps even at preferential prices. He's gone, and suddenly $GOOGL, $AMD and everyone else is knocking on your door with increasingly attractive offers. 

Why exactly would you give NVIDIA the same deal next time?

And remember, Jensen was also helping coordinate the capital needed to keep the whole AI machine expanding. Supplier advances, neocloud investments, strategic partnerships, the lot. 

All while the financial system was already getting more reluctant to fund the next wave of datacenters. Now remove the guy who spent years convincing everyone to invest ahead of demand. 

Jensen's real moat may have been the ability to make an entire industry invest billions today against demand that wouldnt materialize until tomorrow.
